words.etymology: Row from Old English raew ('line'); group from Old French groupe ('cluster, assemblage'); the term is specific to the Parquet and ORC columnar file formats, where a row group is a physical batch of rows that is processed and compressed as a unit.

words.shortDefinition: A storage layout that keeps each column's values contiguous on disk, enabling highly compressed analytical scans.
words.simpleDefinition: A column store (or columnar database) physically stores each column's values together on disk rather than storing all columns of a row together. For an analytical query scanning millions of rows but reading only 3 of 50 columns, a column store reads only those 3 columns' data from disk — a 17× reduction in I/O. Column stores also achieve very high compression ratios because similar values are adjacent (run-length encoding, dictionary encoding, delta encoding).
words.longDefinition: Traditional OLTP databases use a row-oriented layout: all columns for a row are stored contiguously. This is optimal for transactional queries that read/write entire rows. Analytical queries, however, typically aggregate a few columns across millions of rows — they access a thin vertical slice of the table, not a horizontal row slice. Reading all 50 columns to use 3 wastes 94% of every disk I/O. Column stores solve this by storing each column separately, so an analytical query reads only the columns it needs. Additional benefits: data within a column is homogeneous (all timestamps, all user IDs), enabling efficient compression. Run-length encoding (replace 100 consecutive copies of 'US' with one 'US × 100') can achieve 10× compression. Dictionary encoding maps high-cardinality strings to small integer codes. Vectorized execution (processing 1024 values at a time using SIMD CPU instructions) can apply predicates and aggregations on compressed column data without decompressing it. Column stores are the architecture of: Amazon Redshift (columnar on S3), Google BigQuery (Dremel), Apache Parquet (columnar file format), Apache Kudu, ClickHouse, Snowflake. The trade-off: column stores are slow for transactional writes (writing one row requires updating N columns across N column files) and for queries that read many columns per row. Hybrid row-column stores (PAX format, Fractured Mirrors) exist but are not dominant.
words.connector: A column store is like a spreadsheet reorganised by column rather than row: instead of filing complete employee records together, you keep all salaries in one folder and all names in another. Calculating average salary means touching only the salary folder, not every employee's folder.
words.techContext: Apache Parquet stores data in row groups (groups of rows) that are internally column-oriented. Parquet's column statistics (min/max per row group) enable predicate pushdown: the query engine skips entire row groups where no value can match the filter.
words.exampleSentence: Switching our analytics table from row-oriented PostgreSQL to columnar Parquet files on S3 reduced our average query scan cost by 90%, because aggregation queries only read the 2–3 columns they need.

words.etymology: Column from Latin columna (a pillar, column of a table). Store from Old Norse stórr (large) via English. The concept was formalised in Stonebraker et al.'s 2005 paper 'C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS' and independently by the MonetDB project, both predating the 2006 Dremel and Vertica systems that popularised the term in industry.

words.shortDefinition: A compression technique that replaces repeated string or high-cardinality values with compact integer codes referencing a shared lookup table.
words.simpleDefinition: Dictionary encoding builds a lookup table (the dictionary) of all distinct values in a column, then stores each row's value as a small integer index into that dictionary instead of the full value. For a column with 100 million rows but only 50 distinct country codes, this replaces each 2-byte string with a 6-bit integer, achieving very high compression.
words.longDefinition: Dictionary encoding is the most impactful compression technique for columnar storage of low-to-medium cardinality data. The process: scan a column chunk, collect distinct values, assign each an integer code (starting from 0), and store the mapping as the dictionary. Then store each row's encoded value as an integer of the minimum bit width needed. A column with 100 distinct values uses 7-bit codes; with 10,000 distinct values, 14-bit codes. The compression ratio depends on the value size vs. the code size: a column of UUIDs (36 bytes each) with 100K distinct values can be encoded with 17-bit codes — a 15× size reduction. Parquet implements dictionary encoding at the page level: a dictionary page is written first within a column chunk, followed by data pages using bit-packed codes referencing that dictionary. If the dictionary grows too large (Parquet's default threshold is 1MB), Parquet falls back to plain encoding. Dictionary encoding also enables dictionary-level predicate evaluation — for a filter like `WHERE country = 'US'`, the engine looks up 'US' in the dictionary once to get code 42, then filters all rows by the cheap integer comparison 42 == code, never re-comparing strings. ClickHouse's LowCardinality type is a first-class dictionary encoding: columns with < 10K distinct values automatically benefit from dictionary-based compression and vectorized dictionary operations. Apache Arrow uses dictionary-encoded arrays as a native type in its columnar memory format, enabling zero-copy sharing of the same dictionary across multiple array slices.
words.connector: Think of dictionary encoding like a library catalog that assigns every book a short call number — instead of writing the full title and author on every shelf slot, each slot just holds the call number. The mapping from call number to book details is stored once in the catalog.
words.techContext: Parquet's dictionary encoding is applied by default to string columns; when the dictionary grows beyond the threshold (1MB by default), Parquet falls back to plain encoding for the remainder of the row group — you can override this with `use_dictionary=False` for high-cardinality columns where dictionary encoding adds overhead.
words.exampleSentence: Dictionary encoding compressed the event-type column from 3.2GB to 180MB — 98% of the 500M rows contained one of only 12 distinct event types, so each value was stored as a 4-bit integer referencing the 12-entry dictionary.

import pyarrow as pa

# PyArrow dictionary-encoded array

# Manually construct dictionary array

words.etymology: Dictionary from Latin dictionarium ('word list') — a lookup table mapping codes to values; encoding from Latin in + codex ('book') — the process of representing data in a coded form; dictionary encoding describes replacing full values with coded references to a shared value list.

words.shortDefinition: The ordered sequence of changes written by the leader that followers replay to stay in sync.
words.simpleDefinition: A replication log is the append-only sequence of changes (operations or row images) that a leader writes and followers consume to replicate the leader's state. Every committed write appears in the log exactly once, in commit order. Followers read the log and apply entries sequentially, converging to the same state as the leader. The replication log is the implementation of total order broadcast in leader-based replication systems.
words.longDefinition: Replication logs take several forms depending on the storage engine. Statement-based replication (MySQL's older binlog mode) logs SQL statements; it is compact but brittle — non-deterministic functions like NOW() or RAND() produce different values on followers. Row-based (logical) replication logs the before and after images of each row modified, regardless of how the modification was expressed in SQL. It is more verbose but deterministic and handles schema changes more gracefully. WAL shipping (PostgreSQL physical replication) forwards the storage engine's Write-Ahead Log directly to standbys. The WAL contains page-level changes (raw byte diffs of B-tree pages), making it tightly coupled to the storage engine version — standbys must run the same PostgreSQL major version. Trigger-based replication instruments the base tables to write change records into a shadow replication table, from which a daemon forwards them; it is the most flexible (replicates across different databases) but highest overhead. Kafka and similar log-based message brokers are replication logs at the infrastructure level: producers append to a partition log, consumers replay from an offset. The replication log's offset (or LSN in PostgreSQL, binlog position in MySQL) is the synchronization primitive — a follower communicates its progress as a log position, and the leader knows how much it is lagging.
words.connector: A replication log is like a flight recorder (black box) for your database: every committed change is recorded in order. If a standby server comes online after a failure, it asks 'give me everything from position X' and catches up by replaying the log from that point.
words.techContext: PostgreSQL's pg_replication_slots ensure the WAL is retained until every subscribed replica has consumed it, preventing the primary from reclaiming WAL space before lagging replicas catch up — at the risk of unbounded WAL growth if a replica disconnects.
words.exampleSentence: The follower connected with pg_wal_lsn = 0/5A000000 and received and applied 2 GB of replication log entries before its lag dropped to zero — the replication log is the entire shared history between leader and follower.

-- Monitor replication log lag (PostgreSQL)
SELECT
    application_name,
    state,
    pg_wal_lsn_diff(
        pg_current_wal_lsn(),
        sent_lsn
    ) AS send_lag_bytes,
    pg_wal_lsn_diff(
        sent_lsn,
        replay_lsn
    ) AS replay_lag_bytes
FROM pg_stat_replication;

words.etymology: Replication from Latin replicare (to fold back, to repeat), adopted in databases for the process of copying data changes. Log from Old Norse lag (a felled tree), adopted into computing for an append-only record of events. The combination describes the specific data structure enabling follower synchronization.

words.shortDefinition: A set of (node, counter) pairs used to track the causal history of a value across multiple replicas.
words.simpleDefinition: A version vector is a compact representation of the causal history of a value in a leaderless or multi-leader replicated system. It stores one counter per node, where each counter records how many writes from that node are reflected in this version. By comparing version vectors, replicas can determine whether one value is causally newer than another, or whether two values are concurrent (a conflict requiring resolution).
words.longDefinition: Version vectors differ subtly from vector clocks: vector clocks track causality of events per process, while version vectors track causality of values per object. In practice, version vectors are used in systems like Amazon Dynamo (and its derivatives Riak, Voldemort) to track concurrent writes to the same key. Each write to a key in Dynamo increments the counter for the coordinating node in the key's version vector. When a read returns multiple versions with non-dominating version vectors (neither is component-wise ≤ the other), the versions are concurrent siblings — the application must merge them. In Riak's default configuration, concurrent siblings are presented to the application for client-side resolution. Dotted Version Vectors (DVV), introduced by Nuno Preguiça et al., extend version vectors with a dot (a precise event identifier) to distinguish writes that would otherwise be assigned the same logical version, eliminating false concurrency detection. Cassandra does not use version vectors in its replication layer — it uses Lamport timestamps (wall-clock with NTP) for last-write-wins conflict resolution instead. This is simpler but cannot distinguish concurrent writes from sequentially later writes with old timestamps (due to clock skew). Version vectors are also used in distributed file systems (Google Drive, Dropbox) to detect file conflicts when edits occur on disconnected clients.
words.connector: A version vector is like a multi-author document's tracked changes — each author (node) has their own change counter, and the version is described as 'Alice: 3 changes, Bob: 2 changes, Carol: 1 change'. If two copies of the document both say 'Alice: 3, Bob: 2' but differ in Carol's count, they diverged after Carol's last sync.
words.techContext: Riak stores a version vector (called a causal context in recent versions) alongside every value. When a client writes to a key, it must pass back the version vector it last read — enabling Riak to detect whether the write is causally preceded by or concurrent with other in-flight writes.
words.exampleSentence: When our Riak shopping cart returned two concurrent sibling values (detected by non-comparable version vectors), we merged them by taking the union of item sets — implementing the Dynamo-paper's recommended client-side conflict resolution.
words.etymology: Version from Latin versio (a turning), adopted to mean a particular revision of data. Vector from Latin vector (a carrier), in mathematics an ordered list. The combination was coined in the distributed systems literature in the 1980s (Fidge, Mattern) as a natural extension of Lamport's scalar logical clock to multi-node causal tracking.

words.shortDefinition: A query execution model that processes a batch of values (a vector) per operator invocation, leveraging CPU SIMD instructions and cache locality.
words.simpleDefinition: Vectorized execution processes data in fixed-size batches (vectors of 1024–8192 values) rather than row-by-row. Each operator (filter, hash join, aggregation) receives a batch, applies its operation to all values using SIMD CPU instructions, and passes the result batch to the next operator. This dramatically improves CPU efficiency through loop unrolling, cache reuse, and SIMD parallelism.
words.longDefinition: Traditional Volcano-model query execution processes one row at a time: each operator's `next()` call returns one row to the parent operator. This produces simple code but is inefficient: for a 100M row scan with a filter, the interpreter overhead of calling next() 100M times dominates the actual filter cost. Vectorized execution (introduced in MonetDB's X100 system and popularized by DuckDB, Snowflake, ClickHouse, and Velox) processes batches of N values per call. The key advantages: SIMD instruction utilization — modern CPUs have 256-bit or 512-bit SIMD registers (AVX2, AVX-512) that can apply a 32-bit integer comparison to 8 or 16 values simultaneously. Vectorized loops align naturally with SIMD width. Cache efficiency — N column values are contiguous in memory (columnar layout), so loading one cache line holds multiple values for the same operator. Reduced interpreter overhead — the overhead of function dispatch and branch prediction is amortized across N values instead of 1. Selection vectors — instead of copying matching rows, operators pass an integer array of matching indices, avoiding data movement for filtered rows. DuckDB implements vectorized execution natively and achieves single-machine throughput competitive with distributed systems on single-node data sets. Velox (Meta's vectorized execution library) is used in Presto, Spark, and other SQL engines as a shared vectorized runtime. Vectorized execution is most beneficial for OLAP queries that scan many rows with few columns — the columnar + vectorized combination is the foundation of modern analytical query performance.
words.connector: Think of vectorized execution like a factory assembly line that processes trays of 1024 parts simultaneously using a machine tool, rather than one person handling each part by hand. The machine applies the same operation to all parts in the tray in parallel — SIMD is the machine, the tray is the batch.
words.techContext: DuckDB's vectorized execution engine uses a fixed batch size of 2048 rows per vector and SIMD-optimized operator implementations; it regularly outperforms distributed query engines like Presto on single-node data because the vectorized columnar pipeline avoids all network overhead.
words.exampleSentence: After rewriting the hot filter loop to use SIMD intrinsics and processing 256 rows per iteration instead of 1, the column scan throughput improved from 800M rows/sec to 6.4B rows/sec — an 8× speedup matching the AVX-2 SIMD width.

codeExample.code:
import numpy as np

# Vectorized execution: filter + aggregation on a column vector
# NumPy uses SIMD internally — this is the Python analogue

amounts = np.random.uniform(0, 100, size=1_000_000)  # 1M values

# Row-at-a-time (slow, interpreter overhead per element)
total_slow = sum(x for x in amounts if x > 50.0)

# Vectorized (fast: SIMD comparison + masked sum in C)
mask = amounts > 50.0          # SIMD comparison: 1M comparisons in ~100 SIMD ops
total_fast = amounts[mask].sum()  # SIMD reduction

print(total_slow == total_fast)  # True — same result, orders of magnitude faster

words.etymology: Vectorized from vector — a mathematical construct of ordered values that can be operated on as a unit; execution from Latin executio ('carrying out') — vectorized execution describes carrying out query operations on ordered batches of values simultaneously rather than sequentially.
